TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- Iraq's Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Sunday tried to allay Iranian fears over a planned U.S.-Iraq security pact, saying his government would not allow Iraq to become a launching pad for an attack on its neighbor. Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, left, greets Iraq's Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Sunday. "Iraq today doesn't present any threat as it used to be in the times of the former regime," al-Maliki told Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad during a Sunday meeting between two leaders, according to a statement from the prime minister's office. "Today's Iraq is a constitutional state based on the rule of law, and it seeks to develop its relations with the regional countries based on cooperation and mutual respect," al-Maliki said. Earlier, Iran's state-run news agency IRNA quoted the Iraqi leader as saying that "Baghdad would not allow its soil to be used as a base to damage the security of the neighboring countries, including Iran." His remarks come as the United States and Iraq are trying to reach a bilateral agreement on how long the U.S. military will remain in Iraq and what role it will play in Iraq's security. But al-Maliki media adviser Ali Hadi said negotiations between Iraq and the United States are in their "very early stages" and were not part of Sunday's talks.  Watch Ahmadinejad and al-Maliki sit down for talks » . "The treaty is purely an Iraqi-American treaty. The Iranians have nothing to do with it," Hadi said. "We will not discuss the progress or the key elements of agreements or disagreements with them because this is an Iraqi issue." The proposed U.S.-Iraqi pact has triggered street protests in Iraq, where many suspect the deal could lead to the establishment of permanent American bases, a long-term presence of U.S. troops and a weakening of Iraqi government control over those troops. Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was the target of a U.S.-backed Iraqi clampdown in Basra and Baghdad recently, has called for weekly protests against the agreement. Al-Maliki and Ahmadinejad met Sunday afternoon, with Ahmadinejad calling on Iraq's neighbors and the United Nations to help restore security and stability to Iraq, IRNA reported. And al-Maliki thanked Ahmadinejad for his call for an end to longstanding U.N. sanctions against Iraq that date back to the 1991 Persian Gulf war. Iran has long called for the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq, which the United States invaded in 2003. Meanwhile, the United States has accused Iran of arming and training "criminal" Shiite militias in Iraq and of seeking to develop nuclear weapons, allegations the Iranians deny. It is al-Maliki's third visit to Iran since he became prime minister more than two years ago. The two countries, which are neighbors, both have Shiite Muslim majorities, and al-Maliki's ruling coalition is dominated by Shiite religious parties long backed by Iran. Adnan Pachachi, a leading Sunni Arab member of Iraq's parliament, told CNN he wanted al-Maliki to call on Iran to stop supporting armed factions in Iraq. "I think this has to stop," Pachachi told CNN. "I hope that Mr. Maliki will make it absolutely clear that Iraqis of all parties, of all sectarian origins and ethnic origins, are strongly opposed to Iran's attempt to interfere in Iraq's affairs." Pachachi, a former foreign minister, said al-Maliki's predecessor, Ibrahim al-Jaafari, allowed Iraq's security forces to be dominated by sectarian and ethnic militias, and that U.S. troops should remain until those influences are weeded out. "In the long run, it is in the interest of the United States to have a secure Iraq and armed forces and security forces of Iraq with undivided loyalty and allegiance to the state and not influenced by sectarian affiliations or party loyalties," he said.

outputs.L1:
TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) — Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki sought on Sunday to ease Iranian concerns over a proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact, assuring Tehran that his government would not allow Iraq to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbor.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, left, greeted Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Sunday.

“Iraq today doesn’t present any threat as it used to be in the times of the former regime,” al-Maliki told Ahmadinejad during a Sunday meeting between the two leaders, according to a statement from the prime minister’s office. “Today’s Iraq is a constitutional state based on the rule of law, and it seeks to develop its relations with the regional countries based on cooperation and mutual respect,” he said.

Earlier, Iran’s state-run news agency IRNA quoted the Iraqi leader as saying that “Baghdad would not allow its soil to be used as a base to damage the security of the neighboring countries, including Iran.”

Al-Maliki’s remarks come as the United States and Iraq seek to reach a bilateral agreement defining how long the U.S. military will remain in Iraq and what role it will play in the country’s security. However, al-Maliki media adviser Ali Hadi said negotiations between Iraq and the United States remain in their “very early stages” and were not part of Sunday’s talks.

“The treaty is purely an Iraqi-American treaty. The Iranians have nothing to do with it,” Hadi said. “We will not discuss the progress or the key elements of agreements or disagreements with them because this is an Iraqi issue.”

The proposed U.S.-Iraqi pact has prompted street protests in Iraq, where many suspect the agreement could lead to the establishment of permanent American bases, a long-term presence of U.S. troops, and a weakening of Iraqi government control over those troops. Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was recently the target of a U.S.-backed Iraqi crackdown in Basra and Baghdad, has called for weekly protests against the agreement.

Al-Maliki and Ahmadinejad met Sunday afternoon, with Ahmadinejad urging Iraq’s neighbors and the United Nations to help restore security and stability to Iraq, IRNA reported. Al-Maliki, in turn, thanked Ahmadinejad for calling for an end to longstanding U.N. sanctions against Iraq dating back to the 1991 Persian Gulf War.

Iran has long called for the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq, which the United States invaded in 2003. Meanwhile, the United States has accused Iran of arming and training “criminal” Shiite militias in Iraq and of seeking to develop nuclear weapons — allegations Iran denies.

It is al-Maliki’s third visit to Iran since becoming prime minister more than two years ago. The neighboring countries both have Shiite Muslim majorities, and al-Maliki’s ruling coalition is dominated by Shiite religious parties long backed by Iran.

Adnan Pachachi, a leading Sunni Arab member of Iraq’s parliament, told CNN that he wanted al-Maliki to call on Iran to stop supporting armed factions in Iraq.

“I think this has to stop,” Pachachi told CNN. “I hope that Mr. Maliki will make it absolutely clear that Iraqis of all parties, of all sectarian origins and ethnic origins, are strongly opposed to Iran’s attempt to interfere in Iraq’s affairs.”

Pachachi, a former foreign minister, said al-Maliki’s predecessor, Ibrahim al-Jaafari, had allowed Iraq’s security forces to be dominated by sectarian and ethnic militias, and that U.S. troops should remain until those influences are eliminated.

“In the long run, it is in the interest of the United States to have a secure Iraq and armed forces and security forces of Iraq with undivided loyalty and allegiance to the state and not influenced by sectarian affiliations or party loyalties,” he said.

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) — Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki sought on Sunday to reassure Iran about a proposed security agreement between the United States and Iraq, stating that his administration would not permit Iraqi territory to be used as a staging ground for an attack on Iran.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad greeted al-Maliki on Sunday during the Iraqi leader’s visit.

According to a statement from the Iraqi prime minister’s office, al-Maliki told Ahmadinejad in their Sunday meeting that Iraq no longer poses the kind of threat it did under the previous government.

“Today’s Iraq is a constitutional state founded on the rule of law,” al-Maliki said, adding that it aims to strengthen ties with countries in the region through cooperation and mutual respect.

Earlier, Iran’s official news agency, IRNA, reported that al-Maliki said Baghdad would not permit its territory to be used as a base for actions that could threaten the security of neighboring states, including Iran.

His comments came while Washington and Baghdad were working toward a bilateral deal governing both the duration of the U.S. military presence in Iraq and the role American forces would have in Iraqi security.

However, Ali Hadi, a media adviser to al-Maliki, said talks between Iraq and the United States were still in their “very early stages” and were not discussed in Sunday’s meeting.

“The treaty is strictly an Iraqi-American matter. The Iranians have no role in it,” Hadi said. He added that Iraq would not review the negotiations, the main points of agreement, or the disagreements with Iran because the matter concerns Iraq.

The proposed U.S.-Iraq agreement has sparked demonstrations in Iraq. Many Iraqis fear it could result in permanent U.S. bases, an extended American troop presence, and reduced Iraqi government authority over those forces.

Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was recently targeted in a U.S.-supported Iraqi security crackdown in Basra and Baghdad, has urged weekly protests against the pact.

Al-Maliki and Ahmadinejad met on Sunday afternoon. During the meeting, Ahmadinejad called on Iraq’s neighboring countries and the United Nations to assist in bringing security and stability back to Iraq, according to IRNA.

Al-Maliki also expressed gratitude to Ahmadinejad for supporting an end to long-running U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq after the 1991 Persian Gulf War.

Iran has repeatedly demanded the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq, which was invaded by the United States in 2003. At the same time, Washington has accused Tehran of supplying weapons and training to “criminal” Shiite militias inside Iraq and of trying to build nuclear weapons. Iran denies those accusations.

This was al-Maliki’s third trip to Iran since becoming prime minister more than two years earlier. Iraq and Iran share a border, both countries have Shiite Muslim majorities, and al-Maliki’s governing coalition is led by Shiite religious parties that have long received Iranian support.

Adnan Pachachi, a prominent Sunni Arab member of Iraq’s parliament, told CNN that he wanted al-Maliki to press Iran to stop backing armed groups in Iraq.

“I think this has to stop,” Pachachi said. “I hope that Mr. Maliki will make it absolutely clear that Iraqis of all parties, of all sectarian origins and ethnic origins, are strongly opposed to Iran’s attempt to interfere in Iraq’s affairs.”

Pachachi, a former foreign minister, said that al-Maliki’s predecessor, Ibrahim al-Jaafari, had allowed Iraq’s security forces to come under the influence of sectarian and ethnic militias. He argued that U.S. forces should stay in Iraq until those influences are removed.

“In the long run, it is in the interest of the United States to have a secure Iraq and armed forces and security forces of Iraq with undivided loyalty and allegiance to the state and not influenced by sectarian affiliations or party loyalties,” Pachachi said.

**Al-Maliki Seeks to Reassure Iran Over U.S.-Iraq Security Pact**

**TEHRAN, June 2008** — Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki used a visit to Iran to reassure Tehran that a proposed security agreement between Baghdad and Washington would not allow Iraq to become a launching pad for attacks on neighboring countries, seeking to ease Iranian fears over the long-term presence of U.S. forces in Iraq.

Al-Maliki’s trip came at a sensitive moment in negotiations over a U.S.-Iraq security pact intended to define the legal status and future role of American troops after the expiration of the United Nations mandate governing their presence. The talks had stirred sharp debate inside Iraq and alarm in Iran, where officials warned that any agreement granting the United States permanent bases or broad military freedom of action would threaten regional security.

Speaking during his visit, al-Maliki said Iraq would not accept any arrangement that compromised its sovereignty or harmed neighboring states. Iraqi officials emphasized that Baghdad would not permit its territory, airspace, or military facilities to be used for attacks on Iran.

The message appeared aimed directly at Iranian leaders, who have repeatedly expressed concern that the United States could use a security accord with Iraq to entrench its forces on Iran’s western border. Tehran has long viewed the U.S. military presence in Iraq as a strategic threat, particularly amid continuing tensions over Iran’s nuclear program and American accusations of Iranian interference in Iraq.

Iranian officials welcomed Iraqi assurances but continued to voice opposition to any pact that they believed would legitimize a prolonged U.S. military presence. Tehran argued that stability in Iraq depended on the withdrawal of foreign forces and stronger cooperation among regional states.

The proposed agreement also faced fierce opposition within Iraq. Followers of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr staged protests against the pact, denouncing it as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty and a step toward long-term American occupation. Sadr’s movement, which commanded strong support among poorer Shiite communities, demanded a timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. troops and warned against granting Washington permanent bases or immunity for its forces.

The protests added domestic pressure on al-Maliki, whose government was trying to balance competing demands: maintaining U.S. military support against insurgents and militias, asserting Iraqi sovereignty, preserving relations with Iran, and managing opposition from powerful Iraqi political factions.

At the same time, U.S. officials continued to accuse Iran of supporting armed groups inside Iraq. Washington alleged that elements of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, particularly the Quds Force, had trained, funded, and armed Shiite militias responsible for attacks on American and Iraqi forces. U.S. commanders frequently cited the use of explosively formed penetrators and other advanced weapons as evidence of Iranian involvement.

Iran denied the accusations, insisting that it supported Iraq’s elected government and wanted stability on its border. Iranian leaders accused the United States of using the allegations to justify its continued military presence and to shift blame for Iraq’s violence.

Al-Maliki’s visit highlighted the delicate position of the Iraqi government in 2008. While dependent on U.S. troops for security assistance, Baghdad also sought cordial ties with Iran, a powerful neighbor with deep political, religious, and economic links to Iraq’s Shiite-led government. The controversy over the U.S.-Iraq security pact underscored broader regional anxieties about sovereignty, foreign military presence, and the rivalry between Washington and Tehran.

Iraqi officials said negotiations with the United States would continue, but they stressed that any final agreement would have to be approved in a way that protected Iraq’s independence and addressed concerns at home and abroad.

## Iraq’s al-Maliki Meets Ahmadinejad in Tehran as U.S. Troop Presence and Iranian Influence Dominate Talks

**TEHRAN/BAGHDAD —** Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki held talks with Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in Tehran amid mounting regional concern over Iraq’s security crisis, the continued presence of U.S. forces, and persistent accusations that Iran is interfering in Iraqi affairs.

The meeting underscored the difficult balancing act facing al-Maliki’s government: maintaining support from Washington, which has deployed tens of thousands of troops in Iraq, while preserving ties with neighboring Iran, a powerful regional actor with deep religious, political and economic links to Iraq’s Shiite-led government.

Iranian officials used the talks to renew their demand for an end to the U.S. military presence in Iraq, arguing that foreign troops are fueling instability rather than resolving it. Iraqi officials, however, have continued to say that their security forces are not yet fully prepared to assume responsibility for the country without outside assistance.

Speaking after the talks, Ahmadinejad emphasized Iran’s willingness to cooperate with Baghdad and said Tehran supported “security and stability” in Iraq. Iranian leaders have repeatedly insisted that Iraq’s violence is rooted in the foreign occupation and that Iraqis should be left to manage their own affairs.

Al-Maliki, for his part, sought to reassure Iran that Iraqi territory would not be used as a base for hostile action against its neighbors, while also pressing for constructive Iranian support in curbing violence inside Iraq.

The discussions came as U.S. officials have accused Iran of supporting and arming Shiite militia groups blamed for attacks on American troops and Iraqi civilians. Tehran has denied the allegations, saying Washington is using Iran as a scapegoat for its own failures in Iraq.

Iraqi political observer **Ali Hadi** said al-Maliki’s visit reflected Baghdad’s need to engage Iran despite American suspicions.

> “The Iraqi government cannot ignore Iran,” Hadi said. “Iran has influence in Iraq, and it has borders, trade, religious ties and political connections. But at the same time, Iraq must make clear that no outside power — whether Iran or anyone else — should interfere in its internal affairs.”

Hadi added that the U.S. troop presence remained a divisive issue among Iraqis.

> “Many Iraqis want foreign troops to leave, but they also fear what could happen if they leave too quickly,” he said. “The problem for al-Maliki is that he needs American military support while also answering to Iraqi and regional opinion that rejects occupation.”

Former Iraqi foreign minister and veteran statesman **Adnan Pachachi** said Iraq’s sovereignty was being tested by both the U.S. presence and Iranian influence.

> “Iraq must have good relations with all its neighbors, including Iran,” Pachachi said. “But good relations do not mean accepting interference. Decisions about Iraq’s future must be made by Iraqis, not in Washington, Tehran or anywhere else.”

Pachachi said the continued deployment of U.S. troops was a temporary necessity only if it helped strengthen Iraqi institutions.

> “The presence of foreign forces cannot be open-ended,” he said. “There must be a clear path toward Iraqi control of security. But withdrawal must be linked to conditions on the ground, because a sudden vacuum could be dangerous.”

The Tehran meeting highlighted the competing pressures surrounding al-Maliki’s government. Washington wants Baghdad to confront militias more aggressively and limit Iranian influence, while Tehran wants Iraq to distance itself from the United States and reject any long-term American military presence.

For Iraq, the stakes are high. The country remains gripped by sectarian violence, insurgent attacks and militia activity. Its security forces are improving but still rely heavily on U.S. military backing for logistics, intelligence, air support and large-scale operations.

Analysts say al-Maliki’s diplomacy is aimed at preventing Iraq from becoming a battlefield for broader U.S.-Iran tensions.

“The central question is whether Iraq can build a foreign policy independent enough to reassure both sides,” Hadi said. “That is extremely difficult when the country is still unstable and dependent on outside powers.”

The visit also carried symbolic importance. Since the fall of Saddam Hussein, Iraq’s Shiite-led governments have cultivated closer ties with Iran, reversing decades of hostility between Baghdad and Tehran. The two countries fought a devastating war from 1980 to 1988, but many of Iraq’s current Shiite leaders spent years in exile in Iran during Saddam’s rule.

That history has fueled suspicion among Sunni Arab politicians and some secular Iraqis, who accuse Iran of trying to dominate Iraq through allied parties and armed groups. Iranian officials reject that charge, saying they support Iraq’s elected government and oppose terrorism.

Al-Maliki’s challenge is to show that engagement with Iran does not mean submission to Iranian influence, while cooperation with the United States does not mean surrendering Iraqi sovereignty.

As talks ended, both Iraqi and Iranian officials spoke publicly of cooperation, stability and neighborly relations. But behind the diplomatic language lay unresolved disputes over militias, borders, weapons flows, and the future of American troops in Iraq.

For Baghdad, the message from Tehran was clear: Iran wants U.S. forces gone. For Washington, the concern remains that Iran is shaping Iraq’s politics and security from across the border. For al-Maliki, caught between the two, the immediate task is simply to keep Iraq from being pulled further into their confrontation.

**Iraq assures Iran it will not allow its territory to threaten neighbors amid U.S. security talks**

**BAGHDAD** — Iraq has assured Iran that it will not allow its territory to be used as a base for threatening neighboring countries, even as Baghdad continues negotiations with Washington over a security agreement governing the future presence and role of U.S. forces in Iraq.

The assurance came as Iraqi officials sought to balance relations with two key powers: the United States, whose troops remain in Iraq as part of a mission to advise and assist Iraqi security forces, and Iran, a neighboring country with deep political, economic and religious ties to Baghdad.

Iraqi officials have repeatedly said any security arrangement with the United States would respect Iraq’s sovereignty and would not be directed against any regional state. The message is aimed in part at Tehran, which has long opposed a large U.S. military footprint in Iraq and has warned against any agreement that could allow American forces to use Iraqi territory for operations against Iran.

Baghdad’s position reflects the delicate diplomacy facing Iraq’s government. Since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, Iraq has worked to rebuild its security institutions while navigating competing pressures from Washington and Tehran. Iran maintains close ties with several Iraqi political parties and armed factions, while the United States remains an important military and diplomatic partner.

The proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact has been a sensitive issue domestically as well. Iraqi leaders have sought to present any agreement as a step toward normalizing relations with Washington and defining the limits of foreign troop activity, rather than as an open-ended military arrangement.

Iranian officials have expressed concern that a security deal could entrench the American presence in Iraq. Iraqi leaders, however, have emphasized that the country’s constitution bars the use of Iraqi territory to attack other states and that Baghdad seeks good relations with all its neighbors.

The negotiations come at a time of continuing regional tension and heightened scrutiny of U.S. military activity across the Middle East. Iraq has repeatedly stated that it does not want to become a battleground for proxy conflict or be drawn into confrontations between larger powers.

For Baghdad, the challenge is to secure continued international support for its armed forces while reassuring neighboring countries that Iraq’s territory will not be used to undermine their security.
